strengths: The proposed auxiliary objective is intuitive and relevant: predicting future representations provides supervision beyond immediate tokens while leaving autoregressive inference unchanged.

The synthetic experiments offer useful motivation. FSP-BCE solves both tested path-star settings, and learned summaries accelerate sibling-discovery convergence across different numbers of components.
The pretraining study is substantial, covering 3B and 8B models, multiple future-target variants, and six downstream benchmarks.
At 8B, FSP-RevLM improves over standard MTP on ARC-Easy, GSM8K, and MATH, while matching HumanEval+ performance. The inclusion of weaker and negative results is helpful.
weaknesses: Essential implementation details are missing. The manuscript does not adequately specify the large-model architecture and tokenizer, reverse-model size and training schedule, whether the teacher is frozen, target normalization, or auxiliary-loss weighting and reduction. These choices are particularly consequential when combining vocabulary-level BCE or hidden-state squared error with token cross-entropy.

The computational comparison is incomplete. Section 4.1 explicitly excludes reverse-model training, but provides neither an end-to-end cost comparison nor measurements of teacher target-generation overhead, throughput, or memory. Restricting MTP to one auxiliary head does not establish resource fairness when FSP uses an additional teacher model; the claimed amortization is not demonstrated.

Evaluation reliability is insufficiently established. Appendix B.3 selects the best temperature separately for each method and task without identifying a held-out tuning split, creating a risk of optimistic test-set selection. It is also unclear whether the three seeds represent independent pretraining runs or only evaluation sampling, so the reported errors cannot establish robustness to training randomness.

The evidence is more mixed than the broad improvement and scaling claims suggest. At 3B, DS-MTP wins on four of six tasks. At 8B, FSP remains below NTP on GSM8K, its MATH improvement over NTP is small relative to the reported errors, and it ties MTP on HumanEval+. The 3B-to-8B comparison simultaneously changes training tokens, context length, and learning rate, preventing attribution to model scale alone. Near-chance 3B ARC results and the large 8B DS-MTP ARC regressions also warrant investigation.

The central mechanism is not isolated. FSP still conditions on ground-truth prefixes, and the experiments do not directly establish reduced exposure bias or selective retention of long-range information. Reverse-context truncation, alternative teacher representations, and ordinary distillation controls would help distinguish the proposed explanation from generic auxiliary supervision. Higher pass@k alone also does not establish greater output diversity.

Novelty and baseline coverage need stronger treatment. Matching forward states to backward-model representations closely relates to earlier backward-state regularization approaches such as Twin Networks, which are not discussed. Related bidirectional methods are discussed but not evaluated, and the random-token baseline is not a direct implementation of the cited lookahead methods. Consequently, the advantage over strong alternative uses of future supervision remains unresolved.

strengths: Future-summary prediction is a plausible and useful pretraining direction. The reverse-language-model target provides a concrete way to supervise future representations using one auxiliary head, which is discarded at inference.

The experiments represent substantial effort: 3B and 8B pretraining, six downstream benchmarks, multiple future-target variants, and controlled synthetic tasks. FSP-BCE solves both tested path-star configurations, while FSP-RevLM accelerates convergence on sibling discovery.
The 8B results provide encouraging evidence: FSP-RevLM improves ARC-Easy from 71.8% to 76.6% over NTP, improves MATH over standard MTP, and matches MTP on HumanEval+.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not establish a favorable compute–performance tradeoff. Section 4.1 explicitly excludes reverse-model training cost, but neither teacher target-generation overhead nor overall training FLOPs, throughput, and memory are quantified. Amortization is a possible deployment scenario rather than demonstrated evidence. Equal auxiliary-head counts do not establish comparable computational budgets, and a compute-matched NTP or MTP baseline is missing.

Essential implementation details are missing. The paper does not adequately specify the large-model architecture and tokenizer, reverse-model training and checkpoint selection, auxiliary-loss weighting and normalization, or data-mixture proportions. These choices are particularly consequential for matching hidden states with an L2 loss. The provided hyperparameter lists are insufficient to reproduce the central results.

The evaluation protocol introduces unresolved uncertainty. Appendix B.3 selects the best temperature separately for each method and task without identifying a held-out selection set, creating a risk of test-set tuning. It is also unclear whether the three seeds represent independent pretraining runs or merely evaluation sampling; the many zero ARC standard errors make this distinction important. Prompts, answer extraction, and benchmark decontamination procedures are insufficiently documented.

The results support narrower claims than the paper makes. At 3B, DS-MTP beats FSP-RevLM on four of six tasks. At 8B, FSP-RevLM loses to NTP on GSM8K, ties MTP on HumanEval+, and improves MATH over NTP by only 0.9 percentage points against a reported standard error of 1.7 points for FSP. The claimed scaling advantage is also confounded by changes in training tokens, context length, and training settings. The unusually weak 8B DS-MTP ARC results warrant investigation.

The proposed mechanism is not adequately isolated. Reverse next-token training does not guarantee that its entire hidden representation filters out unpredictable future information, and FSP still conditions on ground-truth prefixes. There are no decisive controls separating long-horizon supervision from generic representation distillation, such as short-window reverse targets or alternative teacher representations. Higher pass@k alone does not establish increased output diversity, and the downstream benchmarks do not directly demonstrate improved long-form planning.

Baseline coverage and novelty positioning remain incomplete. Large-scale MTP comparisons use only one auxiliary head; multi-head comparisons appear only on the synthetic path-star task. Random-token MTP-Skip does not substitute for evaluating the cited structured future-prediction methods. Related reverse/bidirectional approaches are discussed but not compared experimentally, leaving the advantage of this particular representation-matching objective insufficiently established.

strengths: Predicting a learned representation of future context is a promising pretraining objective. The single auxiliary head is conceptually simple and can be discarded at inference.

The synthetic experiments provide useful motivation: bag-of-words supervision solves the tested path-star problems, while learned summaries accelerate convergence on the modified sibling task with irrelevant future components.
Experiments extend to substantial scales: 3B models trained on 250B tokens and 8B models on 1T tokens, with comparisons against NTP, MTP, DS-MTP, and several summary variants.

The 8B results contain concrete positive evidence. FSP-RevLM improves ARC-Easy from 71.8% to 76.6% over NTP and from 73.6% to 76.6% over MTP, while achieving competitive coding and mathematics results.
weaknesses: The resource comparison is incomplete. Section 4.1 explicitly excludes reverse-model training cost, but provides no total FLOPs, wall-clock overhead, target-generation cost, or demonstrated amortization scenario. Restricting competing methods to one auxiliary head does not establish resource fairness when FSP additionally uses a reverse model. A compute-matched baseline is needed to assess practical benefit.

The improvements are less consistent than the broad claims suggest. At 3B, DS-MTP wins four of six tasks; FSP-RevLM also trails NTP on ARC-Challenge. At 8B, FSP trails NTP on GSM8K, ties MTP on HumanEval+, and improves MATH over NTP by only 0.9 percentage points, smaller than its reported standard error. These results support selective gains more clearly than general superiority.

Evaluation and uncertainty reporting are insufficiently specified. Appendix B.3 selects the best temperature separately for each method and task without identifying a held-out selection set. It is unclear whether the three seeds represent independent pretraining runs or decoding repetitions. The near-chance 3B ARC results and large deterioration of DS-MTP relative to NTP on 8B ARC also warrant investigation.

Important reproducibility details are missing: the large-model architecture and tokenizer, auxiliary-loss weighting and normalization, reverse-model training and freezing procedure, exact corpus proportions, and evaluation prompts and scoring implementation. These choices materially affect both the proposed objective and the baselines.

The proposed mechanism is not established. Reverse next-token training does not guarantee that hidden states discard unpredictable or irrelevant future information, and the forward model still conditions on ground-truth prefixes. There are no decisive controls comparing reverse summaries with generic distillation targets or varying the learned-summary horizon. Higher pass@k alone also does not establish greater output diversity.

Positioning and scaling claims need stronger support. Related bidirectional methods such as BST and Meet-in-the-Middle receive discussion but no empirical comparison. The 3B-to-8B comparison simultaneously changes training tokens and context length, preventing attribution of improved relative performance to parameter scaling. Together with the evaluation and reproducibility gaps, these issues leave the submission below the acceptance threshold despite its promising idea.

strengths: The approach is simple and compatible with standard autoregressive inference: auxiliary future-summary heads and the reverse model are needed only during training.
The experimental investment is substantial, including 3B/250B-token and 8B/1T-token pretraining, multiple future-prediction baselines, and data-constrained settings.

The synthetic experiments provide useful motivation: bag-of-words supervision solves both tested path-star settings, while learned summaries accelerate sibling-discovery convergence across component counts.
There are meaningful positive results at 8B. FSP-RevLM improves ARC-Easy from 71.8% to 76.6% over NTP and improves MATH from 30.9% to 35.1% over MTP, while matching MTP on HumanEval+.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited relative to acknowledged prior work. Twin Networks already align forward representations with reverse-model hidden states, and prior methods cover bag-of-words and learned future-embedding supervision. Scaling this mechanism to transformers is valuable, but the paper does not establish a substantial new technical ingredient or directly compare against closely related formulations.

The compute comparison leaves the practical benefit unresolved. Section 4.1 acknowledges roughly doubled total training compute and excludes reverse-teacher training from comparisons. Equal token budgets therefore do not establish the iso-compute claims made for the data-constrained experiments. Comparisons against longer NTP/MTP training on the same unique data, with teacher training and target-generation costs included, are needed.

The baselines do not adequately test the central superiority claim. Large-scale MTP is restricted to one auxiliary head despite the proposed method using an additional full-size teacher. Multi-head MTP under comparable total compute, alternative future-embedding teachers, and a transformer implementation of the closest prior alignment method would better isolate the contribution. MTP-Skip is not a direct implementation of the cited random-future methods.

The empirical advantage is mixed. At 3B, DS-MTP outperforms FSP-RevLM on four of six benchmarks, and FSP-RevLM does not improve MATH over NTP. At 8B, NTP remains best on GSM8K, HumanEval+ only ties MTP, and several other gains are small relative to reported standard errors. In the data-constrained 8B experiment, FSP-RevLM averages 39.90 versus MTP's 39.78. Claims of broadly stronger performance exceed this evidence.

Evaluation and reproducibility details are insufficient. Appendix D.1 selects the best of 11 temperatures separately for each method and task without identifying a held-out selection set. It is also unclear whether the three seeds represent independent pretraining runs or decoding repetitions. Prompts, scoring procedures, data mixture proportions, benchmark decontamination, auxiliary-loss scaling, representation normalization, and teacher-target generation details are missing or underspecified.

The proposed mechanism is not demonstrated convincingly. Forward training still conditions on ground-truth prefixes, so richer auxiliary targets do not themselves eliminate exposure bias. Reverse next-token prediction does not guarantee that its hidden states discard irrelevant future information; selected attention maps provide only suggestive evidence. Future-horizon truncation and controlled target ablations would help establish that long-range information causes the gains.

Several interpretations are confounded or unsupported. The 3B-to-8B comparison changes training tokens and context length alongside model size, preventing a clean scaling conclusion. Higher pass@k alone does not establish increased output diversity, and no direct long-form planning, narrative-coherence, or post-training experiments validate those broader motivations.

strengths: The paper addresses an important question: whether richer future supervision can improve autoregressive pretraining without increasing inference cost. The auxiliary head and reverse model are discarded at inference.
The experimental effort is substantial, covering 3B/250B-token and 8B/1T-token pretraining, several auxiliary objectives, downstream benchmarks, and data-constrained settings.
There are concrete positive results at 8B: FSP-RevLM improves ARC-Easy from 71.8% to 76.6% over NTP and from 73.6% to 76.6% over MTP, while matching or modestly exceeding MTP on several other tasks.

The synthetic experiments provide useful intuition: BoW supervision solves the tested path-star instances, and learned summaries retain convergence benefits when unrelated components weaken BoW supervision.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited relative to acknowledged predecessors. Twin Networks already aligns forward hidden states with reverse-model representations, while SemFormer and other cited work provide future-embedding or unordered-token supervision. Scaling these ideas could be valuable, but the paper does not clearly isolate a new technical ingredient or compare empirically with these closest alternatives.

Compute fairness remains a major unresolved issue. Section 4.1 explicitly excludes the same-sized, equally trained reverse teacher and acknowledges roughly twice the total training compute. No comparison gives NTP or MTP equivalent total compute, including repeated training on the same unique data. Teacher amortization is asserted rather than demonstrated, and the later 'iso-compute' descriptions do not establish equal total costs across objectives. Teacher-target generation costs and measured throughput are also missing.

The results support narrower claims than the abstract and conclusion suggest. At 3B, FSP-RevLM loses to DS-MTP on four of six tasks and beats NTP on only three. At 8B, NTP remains best on GSM8K; FSP ties MTP on HumanEval+, and its MATH improvement over NTP is only 0.9 percentage points, smaller than the reported standard errors. In the data-constrained 8B experiment, its aggregate advantage over MTP is just 0.12 points (39.90 versus 39.78), without uncertainty shown.

The evaluation protocol weakens confidence in small gains. Appendix D.1 selects the best temperature from 11 candidates separately for each method and task, without describing a separate validation split for selection. The three reported seeds are not clearly identified as independent pretraining runs versus decoding runs. Near-chance ARC results at 3B and the large deterioration of DS-MTP on ARC at 8B warrant investigation before drawing conclusions about scaling.

Baseline coverage is insufficient to establish superiority over multi-token prediction broadly. Large-scale MTP is restricted to one auxiliary head, although FSP receives a full reverse teacher. Multiple-head MTP is tested only on the synthetic task, and MTP-Skip is not a direct implementation of the cited register- or sequence-based alternatives. Compute-matched, tuned multi-head and latent-prediction baselines are needed.

The proposed mechanism is not established. Training still conditions on ground-truth prefixes, so richer targets do not directly eliminate exposure bias. Reverse-LM training does not guarantee that hidden states filter out irrelevant future information; selected attention maps offer only suggestive evidence. There is no real-world future-horizon ablation or direct long-form planning/coherence evaluation, and higher pass@k alone does not establish greater output diversity.

Important reproducibility details are absent or ambiguous: auxiliary-loss weighting and normalization, teacher training/freeze schedule, target-generation procedure, precise data-mixture proportions, tokenizer, evaluation prompts and answer extraction, and benchmark decontamination. These omissions matter especially for expensive pretraining experiments with modest, inconsistent gains.

strengths: The paper addresses an important question: whether supervision from longer future contexts improves autoregressive pretraining. Its distinction between fixed bag-of-words summaries and learned reverse-model representations is clear and useful.

The experimental effort is substantial, including 3B and 8B models, training budgets up to 1T tokens, multiple auxiliary objectives, and data-constrained settings. Auxiliary heads are discarded at inference, preserving the standard generation architecture.

The 8B results provide encouraging evidence: FSP-RevLM improves ARC-Easy from 71.8% to 76.6% over NTP and improves MATH from 30.9% to 35.1% over MTP. It matches or exceeds MTP across the six reported benchmarks.

The synthetic experiments help motivate the design: bag-of-words supervision solves the tested path-star instances, while learned summaries retain convergence benefits when unrelated components weaken handcrafted supervision.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited relative to acknowledged prior work. Twin Networks already aligns forward hidden states with reverse-model states, and prior methods provide both bag-of-words and learned future-embedding supervision. The broader framework and transformer-scale demonstration are useful, but the paper does not establish a substantial new mechanism or empirically isolate its advantages over these closest predecessors.

The compute comparison leaves the practical value unresolved. Section 4.1 acknowledges roughly doubled training compute for FSP-RevLM but excludes teacher training from comparisons; teacher target-generation costs are also not quantified. An equal-total-compute baseline using repeated data or stronger auxiliary objectives is needed. Calling the data-constrained comparisons 'iso-compute' is misleading without this qualification, and teacher-cost amortization is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Results are less robust than the broad improvement claims suggest. At 3B, DS-MTP outperforms FSP-RevLM on four of six tasks, and FSP-RevLM beats NTP on only two. At 8B, NTP remains best on GSM8K; the MATH gain over NTP and MBPP gain over DS-MTP are small relative to reported uncertainty, while HumanEval+ ties MTP. Figure 6 shows only a 0.12 percentage-point advantage over MTP in the data-constrained regime, without uncertainty.

The evaluation protocol risks optimistic selection and makes uncertainty difficult to interpret. Appendix D.1 selects the best temperature from eleven choices separately for each method and task, without specifying a separate validation split. It also does not clarify whether the three seeds represent independent pretraining runs or repeated decoding. The near-chance 3B ARC results and sharp 8B DS-MTP ARC degradation warrant investigation before drawing scaling conclusions.

The baseline restrictions favor an incomplete comparison. Large-scale MTP uses only one auxiliary head because additional heads are deemed impractical, although FSP-RevLM requires an entire same-size teacher. Multiple-head MTP is tested only on synthetic data. The MTP-Skip surrogate also does not establish performance against the full register-based or lookahead methods discussed in related work.

The claimed mechanism remains insufficiently validated. FSP still conditions on ground-truth prefixes, so richer future supervision does not directly remove the train–inference mismatch. Reverse next-token training does not guarantee that hidden states filter irrelevant future information; attention visualizations provide limited evidence. There is no controlled long-range planning or narrative-coherence evaluation at LLM scale, and higher pass@k alone does not establish greater output diversity.

Important reproduction details are missing, including auxiliary-loss normalization and tuning, precise teacher target-generation procedures, corpus mixture proportions and decontamination, and evaluation prompts and sample counts. Ablations on teacher size or quality, summary horizon, and alternative representation targets would also help determine whether the gains specifically require the proposed reverse-model summaries.
